items.stem: A vendor tells a manufacturing organisation that its AI will 'replace engineers entirely'. Why is that claim misleading for current AI?

options.text: Current AI automates specific tasks but cannot take on the full judgement, accountability and context of engineers
options.rationale: Correct: today's systems are narrow and task-specific; they support rather than wholly replace skilled people.

options.text: Because AI is always less accurate than people on every task
options.rationale: Overstated: AI can match or beat people on some narrow tasks; the real limit is scope, judgement and accountability.

options.text: Because regulations forbid any use of AI in the field
options.rationale: Inaccurate: most uses are permitted with appropriate controls; the claim's problem is overreach, not legality.

options.text: Because AI only works in laboratories, never in real settings
options.rationale: Inaccurate: AI is deployed in real settings; the issue is the breadth of the 'replace entirely' claim.

items.explanation: Correct: today's systems are narrow and task-specific; they support rather than wholly replace skilled people.

items.stem: Which TWO are realistic near-term uses of AI in manufacturing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Predicting equipment failures from sensor data so maintenance can be scheduled
options.rationale: Correct: predicting equipment failures from sensor data so maintenance can be scheduled is an established, task-specific application today.

options.text: Flagging defects on a production line for an inspector to confirm
options.rationale: Correct: flagging defects on a production line for an inspector to confirm is a realistic current application with human oversight.

options.text: Running a fully autonomous factory that never needs human engineers
options.rationale: Overclaim: this presumes general autonomy that current AI does not reliably provide.

options.text: Eliminating all defects and downtime permanently with one AI system
options.rationale: Overclaim: this treats a speculative future capability as if it were available now.

items.explanation: Correct: predicting equipment failures from sensor data so maintenance can be scheduled is an established, task-specific application today.

items.stem: Why must a manufacturing team validate AI outputs before relying on them for a decision that affects a person?

options.text: AI can produce confident but wrong outputs, and sensor data can be noisy and rare failure modes may be absent from training data, so a person must check them in context
options.rationale: Correct: models can err and reflect data flaws; accountable human review protects the people affected.

options.text: Validation is only needed while the model is new; once deployed it no longer makes mistakes
options.rationale: Incorrect: performance can drift and inputs change, so ongoing checking is required.

options.text: Because AI outputs are copyrighted and cannot be used without review
options.rationale: Not the issue here: the concern is reliability and harm, not copyright.

options.text: Validation is unnecessary if the vendor reports high accuracy
options.rationale: Incorrect: headline accuracy does not tell you how errors fall on individual people.

items.explanation: Correct: models can err and reflect data flaws; accountable human review protects the people affected.
